title: No. 21 — Other Defects of the Present Confederation (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Having taken a summary review in the last three numbers of the principal circumstances and events that have shaped the character and fate of other confederate governments, I will now proceed to enumerate the most important defects that have so far disappointed our hopes from the system established among ourselves. To form a sound and satisfactory judgment of the proper remedy, we absolutely must be well acquainted with the extent and severity of the disease.

The next most obvious defect of the existing Confederation is the total lack of a SANCTION for its laws. The United States as now composed has no power to compel obedience or to punish disobedience to its resolutions, whether by financial penalties, by suspending or stripping privileges, or by any other constitutional means. There is no express delegation of authority to it to use force against delinquent members. If such a right were imputed to the federal head as flowing from the nature of the social compact between the States, it must be by inference and construction, in the face of that part of the second article that declares "that each State shall retain every power, jurisdiction, and right, not EXPRESSLY delegated to the United States in Congress assembled." There is, no doubt, a striking absurdity in supposing that no such right exists, but we are reduced to a dilemma. We must either accept that supposition, preposterous as it may seem, or contradict and explain away a provision that has lately been a repeated theme of praise from those who oppose the new Constitution, and the absence of which from that plan has been the subject of much plausible criticism and severe censure. If we are unwilling to weaken the force of this celebrated provision, we must conclude that the United States offers the extraordinary spectacle of a government with not even the shadow of constitutional power to enforce its own laws. From the examples cited, it will appear that the American Confederacy in this respect stands set apart from every other institution of its kind, and presents a new and unparalleled phenomenon in the political world.

The lack of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another major flaw in the federal plan. There is nothing of this kind declared in the articles that compose it. To imply a tacit guaranty from considerations of utility would be an even more flagrant departure from the clause just mentioned than to imply a tacit power of coercion from the same considerations. The lack of a guaranty, though it might in its consequences endanger the Union, does not so immediately attack its existence as the lack of a constitutional sanction for its laws.

Without a guaranty, we must give up the help to be drawn from the Union in repelling those domestic dangers that may sometimes threaten the existence of the State constitutions. Usurpation may rear its head in each State and trample on the people's liberties, while the national government could legally do nothing more than watch its encroachments with indignation and regret. A successful faction may set up a tyranny on the ruins of order and law, while no help could constitutionally be given by the Union to the friends and supporters of the government. The stormy situation from which Massachusetts has only just emerged proves that dangers of this kind are not merely speculative. Who can say what the outcome of her recent convulsions might have been if the malcontents had been led by a Caesar or a Cromwell? Who can predict what effect a despotism established in Massachusetts would have on the liberties of New Hampshire or Rhode Island, of Connecticut or New York?

Excessive pride in State importance has led some minds to object to a guaranty in the federal government as an officious meddling in the domestic affairs of the members. A scruple of this kind would deprive us of one of the chief advantages to be expected from union, and can only come from a misunderstanding of the provision itself. It would be no obstacle to reforms of a State constitution by a majority of the people in a legal and peaceable way. That right would remain undiminished. The guaranty could only operate against changes effected by violence. Toward preventing calamities of this kind, no number of checks is too many. The peace of society and the stability of government depend absolutely on the effectiveness of the precautions taken in this respect. Where the whole power of the government is in the hands of the people, there is the less excuse for using violent remedies for partial or occasional disorders of the State. The natural cure for misadministration in a popular or representative constitution is a change of men. A guaranty by national authority would be aimed as much against the usurpations of rulers as against the unrest and outrages of faction and sedition in the community.

The principle of regulating the contributions of the States to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation. Its incompatibility with an adequate supply of national needs has already been pointed out, and has been amply shown by the trial that has been made of it. I speak of it now solely with a view to equality among the States. Anyone who has been used to considering the circumstances that produce and constitute national wealth must be satisfied that there is no common standard or barometer by which its degree can be measured. Neither the value of lands nor the number of people, both of which have been proposed in turn as the rule of State contributions, has any claim to being a fair representative. If we compare the wealth of the United Netherlands with that of Russia or Germany, or even of France, and at the same time compare the total value of lands and the aggregate population of that small district with the total value of lands and the aggregate population of the immense regions of any of those three countries, we will see at once that there is no comparison between the proportion of either of these two factors and the relative wealth of those nations. If the same parallel were drawn between several American States, it would yield a similar result. Compare Virginia with North Carolina, Pennsylvania with Connecticut, or Maryland with New Jersey, and we will be convinced that the relative ability of those States in raising revenue bears little or no analogy to their comparative stock of lands or to their comparative population. The point may be illustrated equally well by a similar process between the counties of the same State. No one familiar with the State of New York will doubt that the active wealth of King's County bears a much greater proportion to that of Montgomery than would appear if we took either the total value of lands or the total number of people as a criterion!

The wealth of nations depends on an infinite variety of causes. Situation, soil, climate, the nature of the products, the nature of the government, the genius of the citizens, the degree of information they possess, the state of commerce, of arts, of industry — these circumstances and many more, too complex, minute, or accidental to specify, cause differences in the relative opulence and riches of different countries that are hardly conceivable. The clear consequence is that there can be no common measure of national wealth, and therefore no general or fixed rule by which a state's ability to pay taxes can be determined. The attempt, then, to regulate the contributions of the members of a confederacy by any such rule must inevitably produce glaring inequality and extreme oppression.

This inequality alone would be enough in America to bring about the eventual destruction of the Union, if any way of enforcing compliance with its requisitions could be devised. The suffering States would not long agree to remain associated on a principle that distributes the public burdens with so unequal a hand, and that was calculated to impoverish and oppress the citizens of some States, while those of others would scarcely be aware of the small share of the weight they were required to bear. This, however, is an evil inseparable from the principle of quotas and requisitions.

There is no way to avoid this inconvenience except by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way. Imposts, excises, and in general all duties on articles of consumption may be compared to a fluid that will, in time, find its level with the means of paying them. The amount each citizen contributes will to some degree be at his own option, and can be regulated by attention to his resources. The rich may be extravagant; the poor can be frugal. Private oppression can always be avoided by a judicious selection of objects fit for such impositions. If inequalities arise in some States from duties on particular objects, they will in all likelihood be balanced by proportional inequalities in other States from the duties on other objects. In the course of time and events, an equilibrium, as far as it is attainable in so complex a subject, will be established everywhere. Or, if inequalities should still exist, they would not be so great in degree, so uniform in operation, or so odious in appearance as those that would inevitably spring from quotas, on any scale that could possibly be devised.

It is a marked advantage of taxes on articles of consumption that they contain in their own nature a security against excess. They prescribe their own limit, which cannot be exceeded without defeating the goal proposed, namely an increase of revenue. Applied to this object, the saying is as true as it is witty: "in political arithmetic, two and two do not always make four." If duties are too high, they reduce consumption; collection is evaded; and the yield to the treasury is not as great as when they are kept within proper and moderate bounds. This forms a complete barrier against any material oppression of the citizens by taxes of this class, and is itself a natural limit on the power of imposing them.

Impositions of this kind usually fall under the heading of indirect taxes, and must for a long time form the chief part of the revenue raised in this country. Direct taxes, which mainly relate to land and buildings, may admit of a rule of apportionment. Either the value of land or the number of people may serve as a standard. The state of agriculture and the populousness of a country have been considered as nearly connected with each other. As a rule for the purpose intended, numbers, with a view to simplicity and certainty, are entitled to preference. In every country it is a Herculean task to obtain a valuation of the land; in a country imperfectly settled and progressive in improvement, the difficulties are increased almost to impracticability. The expense of an accurate valuation is, in all situations, a formidable objection. In a branch of taxation where no limits to the discretion of the government are to be found in the nature of things, fixing a definite rule, not incompatible with the end, may be attended with fewer inconveniences than leaving that discretion entirely at large.
